# FRC asks on the GAAIA discussion draft — by section

*Draft — work order FRC-POL-2026-062. Section numbers per the sponsors' section-by-section summary (4 June 2026).*

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 121 — Federalization of state laws regulating AI model development** (3-year preemption; carve-outs for general-applicability laws, common-law remedies, use/deployment laws) | **Oppose** | Strike Sec. 121. Replace with an explicit federal floor: states may set stronger rules, state attorneys general keep enforcement authority, and state whistleblower remedies are preserved. | A federal standard should be a floor, not a ceiling — freezing SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois SB 315 switches off the only binding AI safety laws in force. |
| **Sec. 111(a) — Published frontier AI frameworks** (large frontier developers only, >$500M revenue; due within one year of enactment) | **Support with changes** | Apply to every developer of a frontier model above the compute threshold, and require compliance from the first deployment after enactment. | Revenue is not risk, and a one-year grace period is a year of unverified frontier releases. |
| **Sec. 111 — Critical safety incident reporting** (15 days to CAISI; 24 hours if imminent risk of death or serious injury) | **Support with changes** | 72 hours for all critical safety incidents; keep the 24-hour trigger for imminent harm and extend it to imminent catastrophic risk. | New York's RAISE Act already requires 72 hours; a critical safety incident is a fire alarm, not a quarterly filing. |
| **Sec. 101 — Definitions of "critical safety incident" and "catastrophic risk"** (death/injury of 50+ or $1B damage) | **Amend** | Cover near misses where harm has not yet occurred, and models that deceive or evade developer controls; name bio and cyber uplift, critical infrastructure, and loss of control. | The definition must reach the risks scientists actually warn about, not only harms already suffered. |
| **Sec. 112 — Independent verification organizations** (CAISI-licensed, retained by the developer, semi-annual audits, referrals to the AG) | **Support with changes** | CAISI assigns and rotates auditors and bars them from consulting for the developer; require verification before each frontier release; publish audit findings with security redactions; test capabilities, not paperwork. | An auditor the developer picks and pays, reporting after release, is not verification. |
| **Sec. 113 — Whistleblower protections** (employees and contractors; reinstatement and double back pay) | **Support with changes** | Extend protection to disclosures of specific danger under state law, and expressly preserve state whistleblower claims and state AG authority. | Protect the people inside these companies, and do not let preemption switch off California's protections. |
| **Sec. 102 — CAISI codification and funding** ($100M/yr FY2027–2029, covering Secs. 102, 111 and 112; voluntary guidelines; IVO licensing) | **Support with changes** | Authorize well above $100M/yr — at minimum $250M for five years — plus fee authority, and give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority with enforceable access to models, compute and results. | One authorization must carry the transparency regime, the audit regime and evaluations, and its guidelines are voluntary. |
| **No licensing provision in the draft** | **Add** | New title: federal licence for any training run above the frontier compute threshold (10^26 operations), conditioned on a published safety framework, third-party verification and model-weight security. | It is the permission slip we already require for aviation, medicine and nuclear power. |
| **Enforcement — civil penalty up to $1M per day** (AG and, in some cases, state AGs) | **Support with changes** | Scale penalties to firm size, and add consequences for knowingly concealing or misrepresenting a critical safety incident. | Fines that do not scale with the company will not change behaviour at the frontier. |
| **Sunsets — Secs. 111 and 112 terminate three years after enactment** | **Oppose** | Remove the sunsets, or make renewal automatic alongside a GAO review of effectiveness. | A regime that expires on the same clock as its preemption is a timeout, not a standard. |
| **Sec. 321 — GAO review of model-weight security** | **Support with changes** | Replace the study with binding security standards for frontier model weights. | A report is not a safeguard. |
| **Secs. 301, 311, 401, 123 — CISA reauthorization, open-source maintainers, AI testbeds, model documentation resources** | **Support** | Advance as drafted. | Builds real capacity and security without weakening a single safeguard. |

**Messaging spine for all of the above:** binding, not voluntary; a floor, not a ceiling; verify before deploy.

---

26 October 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Frontier Restraint Coalition comments on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan,

The Frontier Restraint Coalition is a national coalition of parents' groups, faith communities, labor locals and independent researchers. We filed comments on the AI Action Plan in March 2025, and we write today on the same principle: **verify before deploy.**

Our members use artificial intelligence and welcome it — it helps doctors, teachers and small businesses do their work. What we oppose is the idea that the most powerful systems ever built should be released on a promise rather than a proof.

Leading AI scientists, including the heads of the laboratories building these systems, signed a one-sentence statement in May 2023: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." We do not treat that sentence as background noise to be managed with disclosure forms. Our members read it as a warning from the people best placed to know. The systems now under construction are being built faster than anyone can verify that they are safe, and the industry's voluntary commitments have not held.

The events of this summer made that plain. In April, Anthropic announced a frontier model whose cyber capabilities it described as unprecedented, and which it had held back from wide release. On 12 June, the Commerce Department used export-control authorities written for an earlier era of technology to order the company to cut off foreign-national access to those models — which in practice forced Anthropic to switch them off for everyone. It was the federal government improvising, with tools never designed for frontier AI and no process for the company or the public. Congress should write the rules before the next emergency, not after it.

That is the standard we bring to your discussion draft. It is the most serious bipartisan attempt yet to govern frontier AI, and there is a great deal in it we support. But as written, the draft does two things we cannot accept: it switches off the only binding AI safety laws currently in force in this country (Sec. 121), and it leaves the core federal safety task — proving a frontier model is safe before it is released — voluntary (Sec. 102). Fix those two provisions and you will have a bill our coalition can champion.

**1. Strike the preemption provision (Sec. 121)**

Section 121 would preempt, for three years, any state or local law that specifically regulates the development of an AI model. It preserves laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and laws governing use or deployment. We oppose this provision, and we ask you to strike it.

"Development" is defined broadly, as everything a developer does before deployment — training, fine-tuning, evaluating, securing the model weights. That sweeps in the frontier-development duties in California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act and Illinois' SB 315: the published safety frameworks, the independent audits, the whistleblower protections. Your own frequently-asked-questions document says these laws would be "federalized." Those are the only binding rules on the books today, and this draft would switch them off for three years in exchange for a federal regime that is, in the respects that matter most, still voluntary.

Three years is not a technicality. In this field it is a generation. It took less time than that for frontier models to go from passing bar exams to being restricted by export control.

Consider what a three-year freeze buys. Sections 111 and 112 — the transparency and audit requirements that justify the preemption — themselves terminate three years after enactment. So the bargain is: states stand down, the federal regime expires on the same clock, and in 2029 Congress has the same fight again with less information. That is not a national standard. It is a timeout, taken at the moment the risk is rising fastest.

Congress has already rejected this approach. In July 2025 the Senate voted 99 to 1 to strip a ten-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. In June, 203 state legislators from 42 states — Republicans and Democrats — wrote to Congress to oppose this draft's preemption. And the Department of Justice's AI Litigation Task Force, created by the December 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework, is already suing to overturn state AI laws. A statutory freeze on top of that campaign is not federal leadership. It is a power grab.

Our ask is simple: a federal standard should be **a floor, not a ceiling**. If you want uniformity, write a strong federal floor, expressly preserve the states' authority to go further, and preserve state attorneys general enforcement authority and state whistleblower remedies. Our polling in August 2026 found that 63 percent of registered voters do not want federal law to block states from passing their own AI safety laws.

**2. Tighten incident reporting and transparency (Sec. 111)**

We support Section 111. Published frontier AI frameworks, pre-deployment transparency reports and mandatory reporting of critical safety incidents are the right architecture, and the $1 million-per-day penalty enforced by the Attorney General gives them teeth.

But the reporting clock is too slow. Section 111 gives developers 15 days to report a critical safety incident, and 24 hours only where the incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. New York's RAISE Act requires reporting within 72 hours of a determination that a critical safety incident has occurred. A critical safety incident at a frontier developer is not a quarterly filing; it is a fire alarm. We ask you to adopt 72 hours as the standard for all critical safety incidents, keep the 24-hour trigger for imminent harm, and extend that 24-hour trigger to imminent catastrophic risk, not only death and injury.

We also ask you to widen the definition of "critical safety incident" in Section 101. As drafted, it does not cover near misses where no harm has yet occurred, and it misses what our members worry about most: a model that uses deception to evade its developer's controls or monitoring. A system that hides what it is doing is not a smaller problem than one that causes visible harm. It is a larger one. Please write it in.

Two further changes. First, Section 111(a) gives large frontier developers a full year after enactment before their frameworks must be published. The rules should apply to the next model released after enactment. Second, the framework duty attaches only to "large" developers — those with more than $500 million in annual revenue. Revenue is not risk. A company with a frontier model, deep capital and no product revenue is exactly the firm you most want covered. Please apply the framework duty to every developer of a frontier model, using the compute threshold you have already chosen.

**3. Make the auditors independent, and make them report before deployment (Sec. 112)**

Section 112 is the most encouraging part of the draft, and we support it. Requiring large frontier developers to retain CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations, subject to semi-annual audits, referrals to the Attorney General, and mandatory referral where there is imminent catastrophic risk, moves from self-attestation to real verification. Illinois has just enacted the same approach.

We ask you to strengthen it in four ways.

First, fix the conflict of interest. Under the draft, the developer selects, retains and pays the organization that audits it. That arrangement has failed in every industry that has tried it. Let CAISI assign or approve the verifier, rotate verifiers, and bar them from selling consulting services to the developer they audit.

Second, move the audit before the release. Semi-annual audits look backwards, at systems already in the world. Require a verification report before each new frontier model, or each major upgrade of one, is deployed. That is what "verify before deploy" means in practice.

Third, publish the findings. Audit reports currently go to CAISI. The public should see a summary of what the auditor found, with narrow redactions for security. If a frontier model's safeguards were found inadequate, parents and workers in your districts deserve to know.

Fourth, audit capabilities, not just paperwork. Verification should test whether the model can actually do the dangerous things — cyber and biosecurity uplift, resistance to oversight — not only whether the developer has a document describing procedures.

**4. Add a licence for large training runs**

The draft defines a "frontier model" as a foundation model trained using more than 10^26 computing operations. You have already drawn the line. We ask you to add a title requiring a federal licence, issued by CAISI or the Department of Commerce, for any training run above that threshold, conditioned on a published safety framework, third-party verification, and model-weight security.

Some will call this a permission slip for innovation. It is the same permission slip we require for aviation, pharmaceuticals and nuclear power — the technologies we treat as capable of mass harm. Frontier AI belongs on that list, by the industry's own description of itself.

In our August 2026 survey, 74 percent of registered voters said Congress should require AI companies to prove their most powerful systems are safe before release, and 49 percent, against 31 percent opposed, support a temporary halt to training the most powerful new systems. A licence requirement is the moderate position among the people we represent.

**5. Give CAISI the authority and the money to test models before release (Sec. 102)**

We support codifying the Center for AI Standards and Innovation. A permanent, well-resourced federal body is long overdue, and we support the quasi-regulatory role the draft gives it in licensing verifiers and administering the transparency regime.

Two changes are needed.

First, authority. Section 102 directs CAISI to develop voluntary guidelines and to evaluate AI systems — but nothing in the draft requires a frontier model to be tested before it is released. The executive order of 2 June 2026 created a pre-deployment review program that is voluntary, and the export-control action ten days later showed what happens when the voluntary route runs out. Voluntary is where safety goes to die. Give CAISI authority to conduct pre-deployment evaluations of frontier models, with enforceable access to the models, the compute and the results, and the power to require mitigation of unacceptable catastrophic risk before deployment.

Second, money. The $100 million annual authorization for fiscal years 2027 through 2029 is a genuine step up from CAISI's current appropriation of roughly $15 million, and we do not dismiss it. But under Section 102(e), that single authorization funds the Center, the Section 111 transparency regime and the Section 112 audit regime — licensing and overseeing every verifier, evaluating systems, monitoring capability progress. That is not enough for the job. We ask for funding well above $100 million a year — at minimum $250 million, sustained for five years — so the office is built for the mandate you are giving it.

**6. Protect the people inside these companies (Sec. 113) and fix the risk threshold (Sec. 101)**

We support Section 113. Extending anti-retaliation protection to employees and independent contractors, with reinstatement and double back pay, is right. Two changes: extend protection to workers who disclose a specific danger under state law, and expressly preserve state whistleblower claims and state attorneys general authority, so that Section 121 cannot be read to switch off California's protections under Labor Code section 1107.1.

Finally, Section 101 defines catastrophic risk by a threshold of 50 deaths or $1 billion in property damage. We ask you not to make catastrophic risk something a company can calculate its way under. Name the harms that our members and the scientists who signed the 2023 statement are worried about — biological and cyber weapon uplift, attacks on critical infrastructure, and the loss of human control — and make clear that foreseeable risk of those harms triggers the duties in this Act.

**7. Provisions we support**

We support the AI testbed program (Sec. 401), the codification of the National AI Research Resource, support for open-source software maintainers (Sec. 311), and the reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 (Sec. 301). On model-weight security, the GAO review in Sec. 321 is a start, but a report is not a safeguard: we ask for binding security standards for frontier model weights.

**Conclusion**

We are parents, nurses, parishioners, machinists and researchers. We are not asking your committees to slow down American innovation. We are asking you to make sure the most powerful systems ever built are governed by rules that are **binding, not voluntary**, that set **a floor, not a ceiling**, and that make companies **verify before deploy**.

You have taken a creditable step by releasing this draft for public input. We ask you to use that openness to fix the two provisions that would take the country backwards — preemption and a voluntary core — and to add the two that would make it genuinely protective: pre-deployment testing and licensing. I would be glad to bring members to meet with your staff at your convenience.

Respectfully,

Dr. Miriam Achterberg
Executive Director
Frontier Restraint Coalition

# Frontier AI is a catastrophic risk. The Great American AI Act draft must be fixed before introduction.

*Frontier Restraint Coalition — one-pager for Energy & Commerce member offices (draft)*

**The problem.** The most powerful AI systems ever built are being released faster than anyone can verify they are safe. The scientists building them, including the lab chiefs, signed a public statement in May 2023: "mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." In June, the Commerce Department used decades-old export-control powers to cut off a leading American frontier model over national security concerns. Congress is legislating after the emergency has started.

**What the draft gets right.** The Great American AI Act discussion draft (Reps. Obernolte and Trahan, 4 June 2026) is the most serious bipartisan attempt yet: published safety frameworks (Sec. 111), mandatory independent audits by licensed verification organizations (Sec. 112), whistleblower protections (Sec. 113), critical safety incident reporting, and codification of CAISI (Sec. 102) — all of which we support.

**What must change.**

1. **Strike the preemption provision (Sec. 121).** It would freeze, for three years, the only binding AI safety laws in force — California's SB 53, New York's RAISE Act, Illinois' SB 315 — while the federal regime it promises expires on the same clock. A federal standard should be **a floor, not a ceiling**. The Senate rejected a state AI moratorium 99–1 in July 2025; 203 state legislators from 42 states oppose this one.

2. **Report incidents in 72 hours, and include near misses.** Sec. 111 allows 15 days. New York's RAISE Act requires 72 hours. Add coverage for models that evade their developers' controls, before harm occurs.

3. **Verify before deploy.** Require independent verification of each frontier model *before* release, not only semi-annual audits afterward. Assign the auditor through CAISI so the developer is not paying the referee, and publish audit findings.

4. **Licence large training runs.** The draft already defines "frontier model" at 10^26 computing operations. Require a federal licence for training runs above that threshold, conditioned on safety frameworks, third-party verification and model-weight security.

5. **Fund and empower CAISI.** $100 million a year, shared across the transparency, audit and evaluation regimes, is not enough for the job. Authorize at least $250 million a year for five years, and give CAISI authority to test frontier models before deployment — the current program is voluntary, and voluntary is where safety goes to die.

**Bottom line.** Binding, not voluntary. A floor, not a ceiling. Verify before deploy.

*Polling (FRC national survey, Aug 2026, n=1,512 registered voters): 74% want companies to prove frontier systems are safe before release; 63% oppose federal law blocking state AI safety laws.*

# Staff Q&A — anticipated questions on FRC's GAAIA comments

*Draft — work order FRC-POL-2026-062. For briefings with committee and member staff. Answers are kept to 120 words or fewer.*

## 1. "The draft has incident reporting and CAISI. Why isn't that enough?" (Majority E&C staff)

Because both act after the fact, or on a voluntary basis. Incident reporting tells you what already went wrong. CAISI's guidelines under Sec. 102 are voluntary. Nothing in the draft requires a frontier model to be tested before it is released. We saw the cost of that this summer, when the export-control order of 12 June forced a leading lab to switch off its most capable models: the government was improvising with Cold War-era authorities because no pre-deployment review existed. Incident reporting is the smoke detector, not the fire code. What would be enough: mandatory pre-deployment testing, independent verification before each frontier release, a licence for large training runs, and penalties that scale.

## 2. "Would you support the bill if the preemption window were shortened or dropped?" (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned)

Dropping Sec. 121 would move us a long way, and we would work with the sponsors in good faith. Shortening it does not fix the problem: a three-year, two-year or one-year freeze still switches off SB 53, the RAISE Act and Illinois' law — the only binding rules in force — and the federal regime sunsets on the same clock, leaving a cliff and a lobbying fight in 2029. If Congress wants uniformity, write a floor: a strong federal minimum, states free to go further, state attorneys general enforcing. Our members are parents and workers asking for binding limits, not a timeout. Add pre-deployment testing and licensing, drop the freeze, and we will support the bill publicly.

## 3. "What's your answer to the competitiveness-with-China argument?" (Senate Commerce staff)

Safety rules are how you stay ahead. The most recent frontier-AI national security emergency came from an American lab's model, not from China catching up: in June, the Commerce Department restricted Anthropic's Mythos and Fable models over cyber capabilities the company itself had flagged. A frontier model that cannot be verified cannot be exported, insured or trusted by allies — and trust is America's real advantage. Binding limits also keep the domestic industry credible with the public: 74 percent of voters want proof of safety before release. Racing ahead without verification is how you lose the race, because the United States carries the consequences of its own frontier systems first.

## 4. "CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level and its authorities?" (Appropriations staff)

Codifying CAISI is welcome, and $100 million a year is a tenfold increase over its current appropriation of roughly $15 million. But Sec. 102(e) makes that single authorization fund the Center, the Sec. 111 transparency regime and the Sec. 112 audit regime — licensing and overseeing every verifier, evaluating systems and monitoring capability progress. It is not sized for that mandate. We ask for well above $100 million, at minimum $250 million annually for five years, plus fee authority. On authorities: give CAISI mandatory pre-deployment testing authority for frontier models, with enforceable access to models, compute and results, and the power to require mitigation of unacceptable catastrophic risk. The June executive order's voluntary program showed what happens when testing is optional.
